title: A Whole Total
statement: For a positive integer $n$, let $R(n)$ be the set of all rational numbers that can be written as $\frac{a}{b}$, where $a$ and $b$ are positive divisors of $n$. Let $S(n)$ be the sum of the elements of $R(n)$, with each element counted once. Find the smallest integer $n > 1$ for which $S(n)$ is an integer.
hints: Try a small case such as $n = 12$. Instead of listing the fractions $\frac{a}{b}$, look at the exponent of each prime in $\frac{a}{b}$ and ask which exponents can occur.

Each prime's exponent in $\frac{a}{b}$ can be chosen independently of the other primes, so use multiplicativity: write $S(n)$ as a product over the prime powers $p^k$ exactly dividing $n$, where each factor is a sum of the powers $p^e$ with $-k \le e \le k$.

The product from multiplicativity gives $S(n) = \frac{A(n)}{n}$, where $A(n)$ is the product of the sums $1 + p + \dots + p^{2k}$ over the prime powers $p^k$ exactly dividing $n$. Show that $A(n)$ is always odd and that $A(p^k) \equiv 1 \pmod p$. This rules out even $n$ and prime powers, so test the remaining $n$ in increasing order.
solution: For $p^k \| n$ the exponent of $p$ in $\frac{a}{b}$ lies in $[-k,k]$. Conversely, any choice of exponents $e_p\in[-k,k]$ gives $\prod p^{e_p}=\frac{a}{b}$ with $a=\prod_{e_p>0}p^{e_p}$ and $b=\prod_{e_p<0}p^{-e_p}$, both divisors of $n$. Elements of $R(n)$ correspond bijectively to such exponent choices, so $$S(n)=\prod_{p^k\|n}\sum_{e=-k}^{k}p^e=\dfrac{A(n)}{n},\qquad A(n)=\prod_{p^k\|n}(1+p+\dots+p^{2k}).$$ Thus $S(n)$ is an integer iff $n\mid A(n)$. If $n$ is even, every factor of $A(n)$ is odd (for $p=2$ it is $1$ plus an even number, for odd $p$ it is a sum of $2k+1$ odd terms), so $A(n)$ is odd and $n\nmid A(n)$. If $n=p^k$, then $A(n)\equiv1\pmod p$, so $n\nmid A(n)$. The odd non-prime-powers below $39$ are $15,21,33,35$, each equal to $pq$ with $A=(p^2+p+1)(q^2+q+1)$: 15: $A=13\cdot31=403$, digit sum $7$, not divisible by $3$. 21: $A=13\cdot57=741=7\cdot105+6$, not divisible by $7$. 33: $A=13\cdot133=1729$, digit sum $19$, not divisible by $3$. 35: $A=31\cdot57=1767$, not divisible by $5$. For $n=39$: $A=13\cdot183=2379=39\cdot61$, so $S(39)=61$ is an integer. Hence the smallest such $n$ is $39$.
